source: Anand (2026) Testing Polya heuristics on AI math (blog)
finding: System prompts each holding one Polya heuristic were run on LeanDojo math problems with three small models. Effect depended on problem type and on model.
numbers: Prealgebra: nearly all heuristics help, except work backwards from the answer. Number theory: almost none help, except extremal elements. Geometry: largest swings. Best on average: segmentation (split by condition, handle cases). Worst: pattern recognition, induction, pigeonhole. GPT-5.4-nano mostly hurt; Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite up to +6 points; Claude Haiku barely moved. Auxiliary elements in geometry about -25% (GPT) vs +14% (Claude). n not stated.
limits: Informal blog, no n, no confidence intervals, unclear if changes are relative or absolute, results given only directionally.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a fixed heuristic menu has no universal value. Supports preconditions per operator (Schoenfeld critique) and testing each of O1-O5 per problem class and per model, never assuming benefit.

source: Llama-Polya (2026) arXiv 2602.10597, instruction-tuning Llama-3.1-8B on Polya-structured dialogues
finding: Fine-tuning on GPT-4o-made dialogues that follow Polya's four stages gave more balanced stage use and fewer one-turn answers in a tutoring setting. No answer-accuracy benchmark was reported.
numbers: About 32,000 synthetic GSM8K-derived dialogues, full fine-tune, 1 epoch. Stage shares (understand/plan/carry out/look back): Instruct 21.9/7.8/12.9/16.5; polya-v2 31.0/18.9/26.7/23.4; metamath 28.5/17.9/29.8/23.2. Error rate Instruct 41.0%, polya-v2 0.0%, metamath 0.4% (error undefined). Sequential metamath+polya-v2 did worse (forgetting). Six experts rated feedback; task-level feedback about 2.8 to 3.2 of 5.
limits: Training, not prompting. Stage annotation by the authors. No correctness benchmark. Error rate undefined. Tutoring aim, not solving.
agent_relevance: Models skip planning by default (plan share 7.8% in Instruct). Does not show Polya structure raises solve rate. Our S9 look back and S1 understand are not validated by this.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting, ACL (arXiv 2305.04091)
finding: A zero-shot prompt asking for a plan first and then execution (PS), plus detail instructions (PS+: extract variables, compute intermediate results), beats zero-shot chain of thought on arithmetic. This is a Polya 'devise a plan' prompt with measured results.
numbers: text-davinci-003, six arithmetic sets. Average accuracy: zero-shot CoT 70.4, PS 72.9, PS+ 76.7, Manual-CoT 77.6, Auto-CoT 75.9. GSM8K: CoT 56.4, PS 58.2, PS+ 59.3 (+2.9). MultiArith CoT 83.8, PS+ 91.8. 100 GSM8K items: wrong answers CoT 46, PS 43, PS+ 39. Original CoT error mix on 46 wrong: calc 7%, missing step 12%, semantic 27%; PS+ calc 5%, missing 7%. With self-consistency on GSM8K: PS+ 73.7 vs 58.7 without; CoT+SC 70.7.
limits: Old model (GPT-3 family). Gain shrinks on GSM8K. Prompt wording sensitive. Semantic misunderstanding errors not fixed. No test on modern reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Plan-first helps weak models mostly by cutting missing steps and calculation slips, not understanding errors. Matches G11: gains at low complexity are small. Variable extraction is a cheap S1 element.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-Back Prompting Enables Reasoning via Abstraction (arXiv 2310.06117)
finding: Ask a higher-level question first (the principle behind the task), then reason from it. A machine version of Polya's generalise and related problem. Large gains on physics and chemistry, none on simple GSM8K.
numbers: PaLM-2L MMLU Physics/Chemistry: baseline 66.4/70.9; CoT 65/75.3; Step-Back 73.2/81.8. GPT-4: baseline 69.4/80.9; CoT 82.9/85.3; Step-Back 84.5/85.6. Llama2-70B Step-Back 64.8/66.7. TimeQA +27%, MuSiQue +7%. GSM8K PaLM-2L: baseline 75.8, CoT 84.4, 1-shot 84.5, Step-Back 84.3 (5 runs). Physics: Step-Back fixes 20.5% of baseline errors and adds 11.9% new ones. Over 90% of Step-Back errors occur in the reasoning step.
limits: Few-shot demos needed. With GPT-4 Step-Back barely beats CoT on chemistry (85.6 vs 85.3). Authors say GSM8K principles are too simple. 11.9% of answers break.
agent_relevance: Generalise (O2) helps when naming the principle is the bottleneck, not when computation is. Precondition: the class has a nameable principle. It also breaks answers, so G3 testing is needed.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: The model writes its own related problems and solutions first, then solves the target. This is Polya's 'have you seen a related problem' as a prompt. It beats zero-shot and few-shot CoT with no labels.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT3.5-turbo 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated 77.8; PaLM2 80.7 vs 81.7. MATH: GPT3.5-turbo 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3; PaLM2 29.8 / 34.3 / 34.8. text-davinci-003 MATH: 0-shot CoT 50.3, 5-shot 54.0, ours 61.0 (needed a demo). Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1: 16 / 17 / 17, and 19 with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars. Average gain about +4.
limits: Gains are 1 to 3 points on strong chat models. Generated exemplars can be wrong. On code, model over-relies on low-level exemplars. Retrieval beats generation for small models.
agent_relevance: Analogue operator O7 has a small positive measured effect on routine problems. Keep it at impasses or in open mode as the schema says.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting (arXiv 2205.10625)
finding: Decompose a problem into easier subproblems and solve in order. Polya's decomposing and recombining. Large effect on length generalisation in SCAN; smaller on math word problems.
numbers: From memory, not verified: SCAN length split about 99% with code-davinci-002 vs about 16% for CoT. GSM8K gain modest.
limits: Not opened; PDF could not be parsed. Numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Supports O3 decompose, but gains are largest on compositional symbolic tasks. Treat as unverified.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures (arXiv 2402.03620)
finding: The model picks from a menu of atomic reasoning modules (for example 'break the problem into sub-problems', 'critical thinking'), adapts them, and composes one task-level reasoning plan per task type. This is a heuristic menu with a selection step.
numbers: Beats direct answering on 23/25 and CoT on 21/25 tasks (PaLM 2-L, BBH, T4D, MATH). Gains up to 42% over CoT on single tasks; up to 32% over CoT claimed for GPT-4 and PaLM 2. Beats CoT+self-consistency by over 20% using 10 to 40 times less inference. On MATH 74.7% of failures are computation errors. Best on world-knowledge tasks, moderate on algorithmic tasks.
limits: Gains are mostly on BBH-type tasks, not competition maths. Computation errors remain the main MATH failure. Module set chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: The clearest case of a model selecting heuristics from a menu with large gain, but selection is per task type from a few unlabelled examples. Fits our S0 class-level choice more than per-impasse choice.

source: Backward reasoning in LLMs on math word problems (arXiv 2310.01991, 'Fill in the Blank')
finding: Working backwards is much harder for models: when the answer is given and a number in the problem is hidden, accuracy falls sharply. Rephrasing into a forward problem, check-your-work, and a Bayesian ensemble with a forward verifier recovered some.
numbers: Forward vs backward, GSM8K: GPT-4 92.8 vs 38.6; PaLM-2 58.4 vs 10.8; LLaMa-2-70B 60.5 vs 15.2. SVAMP GPT-4 90.5 vs 43.9. MultiArith GPT-4 97.8 vs 54.8; LLaMa-2-70B 95.7 vs 6.3. Rephrase/verify gave 10 to 20 point gains; Bayesian ensembling about 7% over majority vote.
limits: Tests backward problems, not the 'work backwards' heuristic as a prompt. Methods solve different problems (little overlap).
agent_relevance: Our O5 asks for a skill models do badly. Expect weak yield unless the backward step is turned into a forward problem and verified by code. Matches c01 where backward hurt prealgebra.

source: Agrawal et al. (2024) Give me a hint: Can LLMs take a hint to solve math problems (arXiv 2410.05915)
finding: Giving a model a human-style hint (pointer to the key idea, as in Polya's teacher questions) beat one-shot, few-shot and CoT on MATH. Wrong or random hints dropped accuracy below CoT.
numbers: 11 models, 17 prompt variants, all 7 MATH topics. Hinting best for every model type except base models. Adversarial and random hints fell below CoT, which was the worst non-adversarial method. Exact accuracies not extracted (figures not read as text).
limits: Hints supplied per problem, not generated by the model. Numbers not captured. Large models not tested.
agent_relevance: A correct hint helps and a wrong hint hurts more. Backs G1/G4: any direction set by an operator must be checked, since a wrong direction is worse than none. Also supports S1 input hygiene against suggestive cues.

source: Hou et al. (2025) SMART multi-dimensional assessment of LLM math problem solving (arXiv 2505.16646)
finding: Benchmark splitting math problem solving into understanding, reasoning (plan formalisation), arithmetic and reflection, following Polya's theory (appendix). Only title page and bookmarks were readable.
numbers: none read
limits: PDF could not be parsed.
agent_relevance: Polya stages used as a diagnostic split. Could score where our agent fails. Open the full paper before relying on it.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating Strategy Diversity in LLM Mathematical Reasoning (arXiv 2605.09292)
finding: On 80 AMC and AIME problems with 217 human-forum reference strategies, frontier models are near ceiling in accuracy but find fewer distinct strategies than people. Accuracy and strategy diversity are decoupled.
numbers: Models: GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek-V3.2 Reasoner. Single-solution prompt: Gemini 100%, others above 95%. Reference 217 strategies (2.71 per problem). Distinct strategies found: Gemini 184 (2.30 per problem), DeepSeek 152, GPT 151, Claude 110.
limits: Small set (80 problems); strategies coded by humans; one prompt pair.
agent_relevance: Asking for multiple strategies does not give varied ones; default approach is narrow. Supports code-tracked history of untried directions (S3 open mode) over asking 'try another heuristic'.

source: PRISM: Plan before Solving, problem-aware strategy routing (arXiv 2509.24377)
finding: A router chooses between natural-language reasoning, code, tool-integrated and ensemble strategies per problem. No single strategy dominates across question types, and strategies correlate low or negatively. Routing beats each fixed strategy.
numbers: MATH: PRISM 53.2%, +3.1 points over best single strategy (tool-integrated), +2.5 over ensemble. Ablation: CoT 9.5% Pass@1 (5,200 ms); strategy adapter with confident routing 10.0%; plus deliberative routing 17.8% at 6,000 ms and 80 tokens. Benchmarks: MATH500, GSM8K, AQUA-RAT, SVAMP, ASDiv.
limits: Strategies are solver modes, not Polya heuristics. Router is trained. Gains of a few points.
agent_relevance: Problem-conditioned strategy choice beats a fixed one, which is the control layer Schoenfeld asked for. Gain is modest. Low correlation among strategies backs trying one untried operator at an impasse.

source: Improving Math Problem Solving in LLMs Through Categorization and Strategy Tailoring (arXiv 2411.00042)
finding: Classify a problem as algebra, combinatorics, geometry or number theory, then give a category-specific strategy (CoT or program of thought). A wrong category costs much of the gain.
numbers: Categoriser: simple word-frequency network 84%, GPT-4o in-context about 88%, SOTA 92%. Trained on 412 MATH level-5 problems. Strategy via predicted category beat random assignment by 67% but was 29% below using true categories.
limits: Only two strategy types. Small training set. Relative percentages.
agent_relevance: Detecting the class (the precondition) is the weak link. A noisy label loses about a third of the benefit. Check class by running, not by model say-so.

source: Sinha et al. (2024) Wu's Method can Boost Symbolic AI to Rival Silver Medalists and AlphaGeometry (arXiv 2404.06405)
finding: AlphaGeometry pairs a symbolic engine with a language model that proposes auxiliary constructions (Polya's introduce auxiliary elements). A purely symbolic Wu method plus deduction rivals it, and the two complement each other.
numbers: IMO-AG-30: AlphaGeometry 25/30 (100M synthetic samples); reported Wu baseline 10; Wu alone re-run 15; Wu+DD+AR 21/30 on a CPU laptop at 5 min per problem; Wu+AlphaGeometry 27/30. Wu solves 2 of the 5 that AlphaGeometry failed.
limits: 30 problems, plane geometry, formalised statements.
agent_relevance: The auxiliary construction step needs search or a learned proposal, and a complementary method adds more than more sampling. Supports a proposal step paired with code that tests it.

source: Duan et al. (2025) HAGeo: heuristic auxiliary constructions for olympiad geometry (arXiv 2512.00097)
finding: Randomly adding auxiliary points already reaches silver level on IMO-30 with no neural network. Hand-written heuristics for where to add points reach gold, on CPU only.
numbers: HAGeo solves 28 of 30 on IMO-30, above AlphaGeometry (25). New benchmark HAGeo-409 with 409 problems and human difficulty ratings.
limits: Abstract page only; the heuristics themselves not read. Formalised geometry.
agent_relevance: Auxiliary construction can be systematic and cheap when the checker is strong. Use code to enumerate constructions and test, not model intuition.

source: Li et al. (2025) Schoenfeld-style episode analysis of reasoning models; ThinkARM (summarised in SUBFIELDS.md)
finding: Covered by the E06 SUBFIELDS file and the parallel Schoenfeld-episode subfield. Link only: Explore is a branch point linked to correctness; Verify is the episode closest to Polya's look back.
numbers: See SUBFIELDS.md: 15 models, 410,991 sentences.
limits: Not reopened here.
agent_relevance: Link to the Schoenfeld episodes subfield. Reasoning models do few explicit look-backs without prompting.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts (arXiv 2305.10601)
finding: Search over partial solutions with a model proposing and scoring steps. Related to Polya's try several plans, but a search method, not a heuristic menu.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Not read for this subfield.
agent_relevance: Our S6 idea tree has this shape but ranks children by code tests, not model scoring.

source: Cross-study synthesis of c01, c03, c04, c05, c07 (no new source)
finding: Gains are large when the bottleneck is naming the right principle or a skipped step, small when it is arithmetic or reading, and negative for already-strong models.
numbers: Plan-and-Solve +2.9 on GSM8K; Step-Back +7 and +11 points on physics/chemistry but 0 on GSM8K; analogical +1 to +3 on strong chat models; heuristics hurt GPT-5.4-nano in c01.
limits: Different models and benchmarks; not a controlled meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Every operator needs a precondition check and must pay for itself at equal tokens (G7). Do not apply any Polya heuristic by default.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts (arXiv 2406.04271)
finding: Keeps a library of high-level thought templates distilled from earlier solutions, retrieves one for a new problem and instantiates it. A learned heuristic menu with retrieval.
numbers: Over 10 tasks: +11% on Game of 24, +20% on Geometric Shapes, +51% on Checkmate-in-One over previous methods, at about 12% of the cost of multi-query methods on average.
limits: Gains largest on algorithmic puzzles; template quality depends on the distilling model; baselines chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: Recording which operator solved which class (our S9) has a published analogue with large gains on puzzle tasks. Test on our own classes.

source: TU Dresden working paper (2025) Context injection: indexed knowledge base on Polya's How to Solve It for LLM tutoring
finding: Proposes an indexed knowledge base of Polya's heuristics injected into prompts. Only a search listing was seen; no accuracy results found.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The idea exists but no measured result to cite.

source: Plan-and-Solve ablation of instruction wording (arXiv 2305.04091, Tables 5 and 8)
finding: Paper states that prompt wording matters and GPT-3 is sensitive to it; correlation analysis found that writing variable definitions and a plan correlates negatively with calculation and missing-step errors.
numbers: Correlation values below zero between presence of variable definition or plan and the two error types (100 GSM8K items). Limitations section names prompt design effort and semantic errors.
limits: Correlational, one model family, 100 items.
agent_relevance: Suggests the useful part of a plan prompt is forcing explicit variables and steps, a cheap format check code can enforce.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-Back error analysis (arXiv 2310.06117, Appendix)
finding: On TimeQA and StrategyQA, adding step-back to retrieval fixes some errors and adds few. Shows net gain with a small break rate.
numbers: TimeQA: Step-Back+RAG fixes 39.9% of baseline errors and breaks 5.6%; fixes 21.6% of RAG errors, introduces 6.3%. StrategyQA: turns 15.4% wrong into correct, 6.1% the other way; fixes 12.7% of RAG errors, adds 4.4%.
limits: Knowledge QA, not maths.
agent_relevance: Break rate is not zero in any setting, so a revise or reframe operator should keep best-so-far (S5, G6).

source: Self-Discover failure analysis (arXiv 2402.03620)
finding: Structure from selected reasoning modules does not remove computation errors; on MATH most failures are arithmetic.
numbers: 74.7% of MATH model failures are computation errors. Structure helps most on world-knowledge tasks and moderately on algorithmic tasks.
limits: One model analysis (PaLM 2-L) on MATH.
agent_relevance: Pair heuristics with code execution for calculation; do not expect a heuristic to fix arithmetic.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) analogical prompting limits (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: Generation-based self-exemplars beat retrieval with larger base models; retrieval wins with smaller ones.
numbers: Gains on text-davinci-003 MATH of 6.9 to 10.7 points over CoT baselines (61.0 vs 54.0 and 50.3), but only about 1 to 3 points on GPT-3.5-turbo and PaLM2.
limits: The davinci result needed an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars.
agent_relevance: Heuristic prompts help weaker models most; the effect shrinks as base ability rises. Re-measure per model.

source: Sinha et al. (2024) IMO-AG-30 combination result (arXiv 2404.06405)
finding: Combining two methods with different solved sets beat either alone: the union reached 27 of 30, above an IMO gold medalist by one problem.
numbers: Wu&AG 27/30 versus AG 25/30 and Wu&DD+AR 21/30.
limits: Small set of 30.
agent_relevance: Different operators solve different problems, so an impasse operator list with code testing (S6) matches the evidence better than one best heuristic.
